summary:
The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency. Tynwald legislates on these questions itself, and United Kingdom statutes reach the island only by Order in Council rather than automatically.

The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender people to change their legal gender and to have the new gender recognised.

The Equality Act 2017 received royal assent on 18 July 2017 and was largely brought into force on 1 January 2019. It lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited.

A ban on conversion therapy covering sexual orientation and gender identity was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and took effect in 2024. In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first part of the British Isles to prohibit the practice.

In July 2022 a community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. No enactment of that bill is documented in this record.

Partner recognition is established. Same-sex couples have held civil partnerships since 6 April 2011 under the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2), and marriage has been available since 22 July 2016 following royal assent on 19 July 2016. The first conversion of a civil partnership into a marriage was completed within days of entry into force, and conversions required no second ceremony. The Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 is recorded in Tynwald Hansard of 26 April 2016.

As of an August 2023 consultation, couples in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship were not recognised as parents on birth certificates arising from IVF or surrogacy, and no law on the island acknowledged surrogacy. No later development on that point is documented.
tangentialFactors:
The conversion-therapy prohibition took effect in 2024, before any equivalent ban covering gender identity elsewhere in the British Isles, and it was carried as an amendment to a sexual offences bill rather than as standalone legislation.

The island's legislature has a long record of statutory reform on sexual conduct. Private consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with an age of consent of 21, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender or orientation by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3). Until 2021, Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men where the act involved persons under sixteen or took place other than in private, with Section 10 defining private as no more than two persons present and not in a public-access place; in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and the language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral.

The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 received royal assent in July 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2022 by proclamation, pardoning historical gay sex offences committed before 1992 on the model of the United Kingdom's Alan Turing law of 2017. Chief Minister Howard Quayle issued an unqualified apology to gay men convicted under the earlier laws, and in August 2022, on the thirtieth anniversary of decriminalisation, the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992.

Employment protection on sexual-orientation grounds preceded the wider equality statute: the House of Keys adopted an Employment Bill amendment to that effect on 30 November 2005, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, and the Employment Act 2006 (c.21) made dismissal on grounds of sexual orientation unlawful from 1 September 2006. Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage on 9 June 2015 and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, ahead of the 2016 Act.
localsOnly:
Under the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2), same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011, and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination.

The Equality Act 2017 lists sexual orientation as a protected characteristic and defines it to include attraction to the same, opposite or either sex and a lack of attraction to either sex.

The pardons and apologies covering convictions under pre-1992 sexual-offences law run to residents convicted historically, not to visitors: the 2021 Act's pardon covers offences committed before 1992, the chief minister's apology was issued to gay men convicted under the previous laws, and the police commissioner's apology of August 2022 covers enforcement up to 1992.
outOfScopeNotes:
Prison housing is unresolved in this record. The island's only functioning prison, at Jurby, opened as a fully operational facility on 14 August 2008 and holds separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders and vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit. No birth-sex-against-identity placement rule, no trans-specific unit, and no trans-specific segregation practice is documented, so no finding on that axis can be stated.

The outcome of the July 2022 hate crime bill consultation is not sourced here; whether gender reassignment was enacted as an aggravating or qualifying ground remains unresolved.

Parent-recognition status after the August 2023 consultation is not sourced; whether birth-certificate recognition for IVF and surrogacy or any surrogacy law has since changed is unresolved.

No trans-specific violence or killing figure for the island appears in this inventory, and no entry, visa, passport-marker or border-screening rule differential to trans travellers is documented. Access to gender-affirming care, restroom and facility rules, and any official complaint or protection mechanism specific to trans people are likewise not sourced.
